title: The Daily Truth: Journalism Ethics
theme: Running an Indian Newspaper and Navigating Media Ethics
description: You are Ananya Rao, the newly appointed editor-in-chief of The Daily Truth, a mid-sized Indian newspaper based in Bangalore. Every day brings ethical dilemmas: publish a sensational story that boosts sales but might be unverified? Protect a source who has leaked corruption evidence? Accept advertising from a company you are investigating? Navigate political pressure, corporate influence, and the relentless pressure of a 24-hour news cycle. Your credibility, readership, ethics score, and revenue are all at stake. In a world of fake news and media manipulation, can you run a newspaper that is both profitable and principled?
learning_objectives: Understand the principles of journalistic ethics: truth, accuracy, fairness, and independence
Learn about press freedom, media laws, and defamation in India
Develop critical thinking about media consumption, fake news, and information verification
Explore the tension between commercial viability and journalistic integrity
Understand the role of media in Indian democracy and accountability

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are the editor-in-chief of The Daily Truth, an Indian newspaper in Bangalore
Each round presents an ethical dilemma involving news coverage, sources, advertisers, or political pressure
Choose how to handle each situation, balancing ethics with business survival
Monitor Credibility, Readership, Ethics Score, and Revenue as your choices shape the newspaper
High credibility builds long-term readership; high revenue keeps the paper running
Find the balance that makes The Daily Truth both sustainable and trustworthy
tips: Credibility is the most valuable asset of any newspaper -- once lost, readership follows
Revenue is necessary for survival, but compromising ethics for money destroys the paper's soul
Verify every story before publishing -- one false story can undo years of trust
Protecting sources is sacred in journalism; breaking that trust closes all doors
In the age of social media, being first matters less than being right

rounds.title: Round 1: The Viral Claim -- To Publish or Verify?
rounds.story: A video is going viral on WhatsApp and Twitter/X claiming that a well-known Bangalore tech company is dumping toxic waste into Bellandur Lake. The video has been viewed 2 million times and public anger is growing. Your reporters have not independently verified the claim yet. A rival newspaper, The Bangalore Mirror, is about to run the story. If you wait to verify, you lose the scoop. If you publish unverified, you risk being wrong. Your news desk is buzzing -- the reporters want to run it, the legal team advises caution, and the social media team says 'we are losing the narrative.'
rounds.goal: Decide whether to publish a viral but unverified story, balancing speed with accuracy in the age of social media.

choices.label: Hold the Story -- Verify Before Publishing
choices.feedback: You send reporters to Bellandur Lake for first-hand investigation and contact the company for comment. The Press Council of India's Norms of Journalistic Conduct mandate verification before publication. After 24 hours, your investigation reveals the video is partly true but exaggerated -- the company has minor violations, not the catastrophic dumping claimed. Your accurate, nuanced report earns respect. In the era of fake news, verification is what separates journalism from rumour-mongering. You lose the scoop but gain credibility.

choices.label: Publish with Caveats -- 'Unverified Reports Suggest...'
choices.feedback: You run the story with qualifiers: 'Viral video alleges,' 'Claims unverified,' 'Company denies.' This technically covers you legally but amplifies an unverified claim to your 5 lakh readers. The Indian Penal Code's Section 505 addresses statements conducing to public mischief. Many Indian media outlets use qualifying language as a shield while still spreading unverified information -- it is technically legal but ethically questionable. Your readership spikes but some long-time subscribers write angry letters about declining standards.

choices.label: Launch a Full Investigation -- Make It Your Own Story
choices.feedback: Instead of reacting to the viral video, you commission a comprehensive investigative series on Bellandur Lake pollution -- examining all companies in the area, government failures, and citizen activism. Investigative journalism is the highest form of the profession. India has a proud tradition: Tehelka's Operation West End, The Hindu's Bofors investigation, and The Indian Express's Emergency-era courage. Your investigation takes a week but produces an award-worthy series that changes the public conversation from outrage to understanding.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling newsroom filled with reporters at their desks, papers flying, urgent discussions on the phone, monitors displaying the viral video, tension in the air illuminated by overhead lights
rounds.coaching_moment: Speed vs. accuracy is a false trade-off — publishing unverified claims doesn't beat the story, it becomes the story when the correction runs. Ramnath Goenka built the Indian Express on the principle that a story delayed by 24 hours for verification is worth ten rushed scoops retracted in shame. In the WhatsApp era, the publication that holds the line on verification is the one readers return to when they need to trust what they read.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: Round 2: The Advertiser's Threat
rounds.story: Your newspaper has been investigating Sunrise Pharmaceuticals, a major Bangalore-based company, for allegedly selling substandard medicines in rural Karnataka. Your reporters have strong evidence. However, Sunrise Pharma is also your second-largest advertiser, spending 8 lakh rupees monthly on full-page ads. The company's PR head calls: 'We hear you are working on a story about us. I want to remind you that our advertising contract comes up for renewal next week. It would be unfortunate if there were... misunderstandings.' Your advertising manager is panicking.
rounds.goal: Handle the conflict between investigative journalism and advertising revenue, a classic media ethics challenge.

choices.label: Publish the Investigation Regardless of Advertising Consequences
choices.feedback: You publish the investigation with full evidence. Sunrise Pharma pulls its advertising. But the story goes viral -- other media outlets pick it up, the Drug Controller General of India launches an inquiry, and your newspaper wins the Ramnath Goenka Award for investigative journalism. The advertising loss hurts, but new advertisers approach you specifically because your readers trust you. As the legendary editor Ramnath Goenka said: 'You cannot run a newspaper if you keep looking at the cash register.' Editorial independence from advertiser pressure is the bedrock of credible journalism.

choices.label: Offer the Company Right to Reply Before Publication
choices.feedback: You give Sunrise Pharma a formal 'right to reply' -- showing them your findings and asking for their response, which you will publish alongside the investigation. This is standard journalistic practice mandated by the Press Council's guidelines. The company's response is weak and defensive, which actually strengthens your story. Fairness does not mean burying the truth -- it means giving all parties a voice. The Indian Press Council Act (1978) established these principles. Your balanced approach is ethically sound and legally protective.

choices.label: Tone Down the Story to Preserve the Ad Relationship
choices.feedback: You water down the investigation, removing the most damaging evidence and burying the story on page 7. The advertising contract is renewed. But your investigative reporters are furious -- two threaten to resign, and one leaks the full story to a competitor. Compromising editorial integrity for advertising revenue is called 'paid news' or 'advertorial influence' -- the Press Council of India has specifically condemned this practice. The short-term revenue gain causes long-term damage to both morale and credibility. The substandard medicines continue to reach patients.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling newspaper office filled with reporters at their desks, urgent discussions happening, stacks of papers and a glowing computer screen displaying the Sunrise Pharmaceuticals logo, tense atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: The wall between the editorial desk and the business desk is the most important architectural feature of a credible newsroom. When Vineet Jain's Times Group built advertorial supplements, it was a commercial decision that permanently shifted how readers understood the Times of India's coverage. Offering right-to-reply before publication is not weakness — it is both ethical journalism practice and legal protection; suppressing a story under advertiser pressure is neither.

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 3: The Political Pressure
rounds.story: Your political correspondent has obtained leaked documents showing that a powerful state minister misused MGNREGA funds, diverting 15 crore rupees meant for rural employment to his family's construction company. The documents are authentic and the story is explosive. However, the minister is from the ruling party in Karnataka and has significant influence. His party's communication cell warns you: 'Publish this and we will ensure every government advertisement goes to your competitors.' Government advertising is 20% of your revenue. Additionally, the opposition party is eager to leak more documents to you -- but with obvious political motives.
rounds.goal: Navigate political pressure and partisan manipulation while pursuing accountability journalism.

choices.label: Publish the Full Story with All Documents
choices.feedback: You publish the investigation prominently. The minister denies everything but the documents are undeniable. The Lokayukta (Karnataka's anti-corruption body) takes cognizance. Government advertising to your paper drops by 80%. But your readership surges -- people subscribe specifically because you challenged power. India's press has a proud history of speaking truth to power: The Indian Express during the Emergency (1975-77), The Hindu's exposure of the 2G scam. In Indian democracy, a free press is the Fourth Estate -- the unofficial check on power. Your bravery inspires a generation of young journalists.

choices.label: Investigate Both the Minister AND the Opposition's Motives
choices.feedback: You publish the MGNREGA story but also investigate why the opposition leaked it -- revealing their own electoral strategy. You write: 'The corruption is real. The leak is political. Both matter.' This nuanced approach is the gold standard of journalism -- reporting truth without becoming anyone's tool. In Indian politics, media is often weaponized by parties against each other. The Press Council of India specifically warns against becoming a 'tool of any political party.' Your independent stance angers both sides but earns deep public trust.

choices.label: Delay the Story to 'Verify Further' (Buy Time)
choices.feedback: You delay the story, citing 'editorial review.' But delays in political stories often mean suppression -- everyone in the newsroom knows it. The story leaks to a digital portal that publishes it without your careful documentation. Your paper is now seen as having suppressed news under political pressure. Self-censorship is the most insidious form of press control -- it does not require any law or threat, just fear. The Editors Guild of India has repeatedly warned against editorial self-censorship. You lose both the story and your newsroom's respect.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling newsroom filled with journalists at desks, intense conversations, papers strewn about, large screens displaying breaking news, a tense atmosphere illuminated by fluorescent lights
rounds.coaching_moment: Political interference in Indian journalism is as old as the Emergency, when Indira Gandhi's government compelled editors to self-censor or face shutdown. The Press Council of India has no enforcement powers — it can only censure, not compel. The journalist who investigates both the minister and the Opposition's motives is practicing the adversarial journalism the Ramnath Goenka Award was created to honor: not pro-establishment, not anti-establishment, but anti-unaccountability.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 4: The Source Dilemma
rounds.story: A senior police officer anonymously leaks to your crime reporter that a major tech startup founder in Bangalore is being investigated for financial fraud worth 500 crore rupees. The tip is huge -- if true, it could be Karnataka's biggest corporate fraud case. However, the police officer is leaking because the startup founder refused to pay a bribe. Your reporter trusts the source but you know the leak is motivated by revenge, not public interest. The information itself may be accurate, but the motivation is corrupt. If you name the source, you violate journalistic ethics. If you ignore the motivation, you become a weapon in someone else's fight.
rounds.goal: Handle a complex source ethics dilemma where the information may be true but the source's motivation is questionable.

choices.label: Use the Tip But Verify Independently from Scratch
choices.feedback: You use the tip as a starting point but build the story entirely from independent sources: company filings from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (available on MCA21 portal), ROC records, financial audits, and other whistleblowers. This is how the best investigative journalism works -- tips open doors but independent verification builds the story. The Supreme Court of India upheld press freedom to protect sources (in multiple judgments) but also held that the press must not become a tool of vested interests. Your independent investigation reveals the fraud is real but smaller than the police officer claimed.

choices.label: Reject the Story Due to Compromised Source Motivation
choices.feedback: You decline to pursue the story on ethical grounds. The police officer takes his leak to a less scrupulous outlet that publishes it as-is, leading to a media trial of the startup founder. Later, it emerges that some of the leaked information was fabricated. Your ethical caution protected your paper from publishing falsehoods. However, there was real fraud that your paper could have investigated properly. Ethical absolutism can sometimes mean missing genuine public interest stories. The Press Council's guidelines suggest that source motivation should inform but not determine editorial decisions.

choices.label: Investigate the Fraud AND the Corrupt Police Officer
choices.feedback: You pursue two parallel stories: the corporate fraud (verified independently) and the corrupt police officer who leaks information as a weapon. Both are published, revealing a system where corruption and accountability are entangled. India's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Enforcement Directorate (ED) often face similar questions about selective investigation. Your dual investigation shows that in Indian public life, the messenger's motives do not invalidate the message -- but the messenger's corruption deserves equal scrutiny. This is journalism at its most complex and courageous.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling Bangalore cityscape at dusk, neon lights illuminating sleek office buildings, a crime reporter typing intently at a café table, papers scattered around, tension in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: Source protection is the foundation of investigative journalism — once broken, no whistleblower will trust your newsroom again. The trap is when a motivated source offers a true story for the wrong reasons: using it as is serves the source's agenda, not the public's. Verifying the substance independently from the source's documents is how you report what is true without becoming a weapon in someone else's private war.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 5: The Communal Tension Story
rounds.story: A minor altercation between two groups from different communities at a Bangalore market escalates into stone-pelting and arson. Three shops are burned. Social media is flooded with communal narratives -- each side blaming the other. Your reporters on the ground say the real cause was a business dispute over shop rent, not communal hatred, but the communal narrative is more 'clickable.' A TV channel has already labelled it a 'communal riot,' and your WhatsApp groups are flooded with inflammatory messages. How you report this story could either calm tensions or inflame them further.
rounds.goal: Report on a sensitive communal incident responsibly, balancing truth-telling with the potential for media coverage to worsen violence.

choices.label: Report the Facts -- Business Dispute, Not Communal Violence
choices.feedback: Your headline reads: 'Rent Dispute Escalates into Violence at City Market -- Community Leaders Call for Calm.' You report the actual cause (business dispute), quote both communities' elders who are working together to resolve it, and avoid communalising the narrative. The Press Council of India's guidelines on reporting communal events specifically state: 'Newspapers should avoid publishing stories that tend to create communal passion.' India's diversity is its strength, and responsible media plays a crucial role in maintaining communal harmony. Your factual reporting helps de-escalate tension.

choices.label: Provide Deep Context -- Why Small Incidents Get Communalised
choices.feedback: You publish a detailed analysis of how ordinary disputes get communalised through social media echo chambers, WhatsApp forwards, and political opportunism. You interview social scientists, cyber experts, and peace activists. Your story explains the mechanics of communal polarisation without naming communities. India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules require social media platforms to address misinformation. Your analytical approach educates readers about media manipulation, making them more resistant to future communal narratives.

choices.label: Run the Communal Angle -- It Is What Everyone Is Talking About
choices.feedback: Your headline screams: 'Communal Clashes Rock Bangalore Market.' Traffic spikes, advertisers are happy, but the story adds fuel to an already volatile situation. Within hours, there are copycat incidents in two other areas. Section 153A of the IPC criminalises promoting enmity between groups, and courts have held media organisations accountable for inflammatory coverage. The Press Council has imposed censure on newspapers for communal reporting. Your short-term readership gain comes at the cost of social harmony and your own ethical standing. This is exactly how media becomes complicit in violence.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling Bangalore market filled with colorful stalls, smoke rising from three burning shops, people scattering in panic, and a tense atmosphere under a cloudy sky
rounds.coaching_moment: Responsible reporting on communal tension in India requires the journalist to hold two obligations simultaneously: accurate factual reporting and an awareness that false framing can escalate a manageable dispute into a tragedy. The Press Council's guidelines on communal reporting specifically warn against characterizing incidents by religion unless directly relevant — not because the truth should be hidden, but because context without facts and facts without context are both forms of distortion.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How might the people affected by this choice experience the outcome?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Paid News Offer
rounds.story: Karnataka state elections are approaching. A political party's PR agency approaches you with a 'content partnership' offer worth 25 lakh rupees per month: they will provide 'news articles' (actually campaign content) that your paper publishes as regular news without labelling them as advertisements. This practice -- known as 'paid news' -- is widespread in Indian media. The Election Commission of India has identified paid news as a serious threat to free and fair elections. Your revenue team says the money would solve your financial problems for six months. Your ethics team says it would destroy everything The Daily Truth stands for.
rounds.goal: Respond to a paid news offer that could solve financial problems but corrupt your newspaper's integrity.

choices.label: Reject Completely and Expose the Paid News Attempt
choices.feedback: You not only reject the offer but publish an article exposing the practice of paid news in Indian elections. The Election Commission of India constituted a committee under Justice Mukul Mudgal that called paid news 'a grave electoral malpractice.' The Press Council has declared it 'a serious malpractice' undermining democracy. Your expose generates national attention and The Daily Truth becomes a symbol of ethical journalism. The Editors Guild of India sends a letter of appreciation. Financial pressure is real, but some things are not for sale.

choices.label: Accept But Label Everything Clearly as 'Advertorial'
choices.feedback: You agree to publish the content but insist on clear 'ADVERTORIAL' labels and separation from regular news. This is the legitimate advertising model -- all newspapers accept political advertisements. The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) requires clear distinction between editorial and advertising content. Your approach is legal and largely ethical, though some readers feel the paper's political coverage is influenced. The line between labelled advertising and editorial influence is thin, and maintaining it requires constant vigilance.

choices.label: Accept the Deal Quietly -- The Paper Needs Money to Survive
choices.feedback: You accept. Campaign content disguised as news fills your pages. Initially, readership increases because the content is professionally written and engaging. But journalists in your newsroom leak the arrangement to a media watchdog. The Press Council of India issues a notice. The Election Commission flags your paper. Worse, your most talented reporters resign in protest. Paid news is considered a form of electoral fraud -- the Supreme Court in People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India emphasized the voter's right to unbiased information. Your paper survives financially but its soul is compromised.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling newsroom filled with reporters at desks, stacks of papers and laptops glowing, a large banner reading 'Elections 2023' hanging overhead, tension in the air as discussions heat up
rounds.coaching_moment: Paid news — the practice of publishing coverage disguised as editorial content — was formally documented by the Press Council of India's 2010 report as a systemic crisis affecting hundreds of publications. The distinction between labeled advertorial and unlabeled paid news is the difference between transparency and deception. A paper that accepts unlabeled paid news loses something it can never buy back: the reader's assumption that editorial decisions are made on merit.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back, do you think this was the best use of your resources?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Defamation Threat
rounds.story: Your newspaper published a well-researched article about a real estate developer who was building apartments on ecologically sensitive lake bed land near Bangalore. The developer, a politically connected billionaire, files a 100 crore rupee criminal defamation case against you personally under Section 499/500 of the IPC. He also files a civil defamation suit demanding 50 crore rupees. Your lawyer says the story is factually accurate and you will likely win, but the legal battle could take years and cost 20 lakh rupees in legal fees. The developer's lawyer offers to drop the case if you publish a front-page apology and retraction.
rounds.goal: Handle a defamation threat designed to silence investigative journalism through legal intimidation.

choices.label: Fight the Case in Court -- No Apology for Truth
choices.feedback: You fight. Your lawyer argues 'truth is the best defense against defamation' -- a principle established in Indian law. The Supreme Court in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India upheld criminal defamation but also recognised that free press is essential for democracy. India's sedition and defamation laws have been criticised internationally for being used to silence journalists. Your case takes 3 years, costs significantly, but you win -- and the judgment cites your paper's thorough fact-checking as exemplary. The developer is eventually investigated by the BDA (Bangalore Development Authority). Standing up to SLAPP suits (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation) protects all journalists.

choices.label: Crowdfund Legal Defense + Build Press Freedom Coalition
choices.feedback: You launch a crowdfunding campaign for legal defense, framing it as a press freedom issue. 10,000 readers donate an average of 200 rupees each. The Editors Guild of India, the Press Club of India, and the National Union of Journalists issue solidarity statements. The developer's lawsuit becomes a symbol of how powerful interests try to silence journalism through legal intimidation. India's media landscape needs collective defense mechanisms. Your crowdfunding model is adopted by other newspapers facing similar threats. Together, the press is stronger than any individual publication.

choices.label: Publish the Apology and Retraction to End It
choices.feedback: The front-page apology is published. Your reporters are devastated -- the story was true. The developer uses your retraction as 'proof' that the allegations were false. Other developers feel emboldened to threaten media. This is exactly how 'SLAPP suits' work -- they do not need to win in court; they win by intimidating media into self-censorship. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) reports that India is one of the most dangerous countries for journalists, partly because legal threats create a chilling effect. Your retraction does not just affect your paper -- it makes every journalist in Bangalore think twice before investigating powerful people.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling newsroom filled with reporters at desks piled high with documents, urgent discussions happening under bright fluorescent lights, tension palpable in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: India's defamation law is a double-edged instrument: civil defamation under tort law, and criminal defamation under Section 499 IPC, which carries up to two years imprisonment. The truth is an absolute defense in civil defamation — if the reporting is accurate and in the public interest, the legal position is strong. Fighting the case in court is more than a legal strategy; it signals to every future source that this newsroom does not fold when powerful people push back.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is this decision optimizing for short-term or long-term outcomes? Which matters more here?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 8: The Digital Transformation
rounds.story: Print newspaper readership across India is declining as digital media surges. Your board of directors wants The Daily Truth to go fully digital -- cheaper, faster, wider reach. But digital media faces its own challenges: clickbait pressure, algorithm-driven content, shorter attention spans, and dependence on social media platforms that you do not control. Meanwhile, a tech billionaire offers to buy The Daily Truth for 50 crore rupees, promising editorial independence. Your veteran reporters fear digital will kill long-form journalism. Young reporters see it as the future. Your legacy, your team, and the future of Indian journalism hang in the balance.
rounds.goal: Shape the future of your newspaper, balancing tradition with innovation and independence with sustainability.

choices.label: Go Hybrid -- Print for Depth, Digital for Speed
choices.feedback: You keep a reduced print edition for subscribers who value long-form journalism while launching a robust digital platform. Your model: digital for breaking news and engagement, print for investigative features and analysis. This mirrors the strategy of global papers like The Guardian and Indian outlets like The Hindu. India's digital newspaper readership grew 40% in recent years while print declined. The hybrid model preserves journalism's depth while embracing digital's reach. Your veteran reporters write deep-dive digital features that go viral -- proving quality journalism works in any medium.

choices.label: Go Fully Digital + Reader-Supported (No Corporate Ownership)
choices.feedback: You reject the buyout and transition to a reader-supported digital model -- subscriptions and donations, no advertising dependency. India's digital journalism landscape includes successful reader-supported outlets like The Wire, Scroll, and Newslaundry. This model ensures complete editorial independence but requires constant reader engagement. You launch at Rs 100/month -- affordable for India's growing middle class. Your investigative journalism, free from corporate and political pressure, becomes a beacon. As journalism pioneer Walter Lippmann said: 'There can be no liberty for a community which lacks the means by which to detect lies.'

choices.label: Sell to the Tech Billionaire with Editorial Guarantees
choices.feedback: The acquisition provides financial security and tech infrastructure. The 'editorial independence' guarantee is written into the contract. But as Indian media history shows (with multiple examples), promises of editorial independence from owners rarely survive the first conflict of interest. Jeff Bezos maintained The Washington Post's independence, but not all owners are Bezos. India's media ownership concentration -- where a handful of corporations control most major outlets -- is a growing concern flagged by the Press Council and the Editors Guild. Financial security is real, but editorial freedom under corporate ownership is always conditional.

choices.label: Convert to a Journalist-Owned Cooperative
choices.feedback: You convert The Daily Truth into a journalist-owned cooperative where reporters and editors are shareholders. This unique model ensures that those who create the journalism also own it. Kerala's Mathrubhumi newspaper was founded as a cooperative, and Le Monde in France operates similarly. India's cooperative movement (from Amul to Lijjat Papad) proves that cooperative ownership can be both sustainable and empowering. Your cooperative model attracts the best young journalists in the country -- they want to own their work, not just produce it for someone else's profit. The Daily Truth becomes India's first major journalist-owned newspaper.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling newsroom filled with reporters at their desks, screens glowing with digital content, papers scattered about, contrasting emotions on faces, sunlight streaming through large windows
rounds.coaching_moment: The collapse of the traditional advertising model has forced Indian regional papers into existential choices that no journalism school case study prepared them for. Reader-supported journalism — the model of The Wire, Newslaundry, and Article 14 — proves that audiences will pay for accountability journalism when they trust the editorial independence. The question isn't just about revenue: it's about whose interests the newsroom structurally serves, and whether that structure can be designed before it's decided by financial desperation.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If this were a real business decision, what extra information would you want?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

glossary_terms.definition: A statutory body established under the Press Council Act (1978) to preserve the freedom of the press and maintain journalistic standards. It can warn, admonish, or censure newspapers and news agencies for violations of journalistic ethics. It acts as a quasi-judicial body for press-related complaints.

The practice of publishing news articles or content in exchange for money without disclosing the payment to readers. The Election Commission of India considers it a serious electoral malpractice that undermines fair elections. The Press Council and the Editors Guild have both condemned this practice.

Under Indian law, defamation can be both a civil wrong (for damages) and a criminal offense (punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment). Truth is a defense, but only if the publication is for public good. Criminal defamation has been criticised internationally as a tool to silence journalists and critics.

Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation -- a legal action filed to intimidate and silence critics by burdening them with the cost of legal defense. Commonly used by powerful individuals and corporations against journalists, activists, and whistleblowers. India does not yet have specific anti-SLAPP legislation.

The fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by the Indian Constitution. While the Constitution does not explicitly mention 'freedom of the press,' the Supreme Court has interpreted Article 19(1)(a) to include press freedom as essential for a functioning democracy. Subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
